title: Karisma Kapoor Went to Kolkata in Peak Summer and Came Back With the Role of Her Life.
excerpt: Brown is messy, divisive, and sometimes too in love with its own darkness. But Karisma as whisky-soaked detective Rita Brown is the single best performance streaming on Indian OTT right now.
body:
She said no. The production team showed up at Mehboob Studios while she was shooting an ad, refused to leave, and waited until she agreed to at least read the script. That's how Karisma Kapoor ended up spending 50 days in Kolkata's worst summer heat, sweating through take after take as a disgraced, alcoholic Anglo-Indian detective named Rita Brown.

And that's how she delivered the most textured, quietly devastating performance of a career that already includes two National Awards.

Brown, now streaming on ZEE5 (premiered June 5), is adapted from Abheek Barua's 2016 novel City of Death and directed by Abhinay Deo (24: India). It follows DCP Rita Brown — once Kolkata's finest, now suspended, grief-hollowed, reaching for the whisky before the alarm clock. When the daughter of a powerful industrialist turns up murdered, Rita is pulled back into the force for what the show makes clear from its opening frame is her last shot at redemption.

"Rita Brown is unlike any character I've played before. Her strength lies in her fragility and silence as much as in her courage. There's no attempt to glamorise pain." — Karisma Kapoor

The Performance That Outran the Show

Here is the uncomfortable truth about Brown: critics cannot agree on whether the series works, but they are nearly unanimous that Karisma does.

India Today gave it 3.5 stars, calling it a "psychological crime drama that relies more on its characters and mood than on shock value." The Times of India matched that rating, recommending it for fans of "atmospheric slow-burn crime thrillers." Scroll.in praised its "well-written characters with defined arcs." Rediff went with 3.5 stars and called Karisma's return "powerful."

But The Indian Express dropped a flat 2 out of 5, calling it "cliche-ridden." India Forums labelled it "dark, dreary and disappointingly hollow." Bollywood Hungama landed at 2 stars, noting that the series is "let down by predictable twists and inconsistent writing."

The through-line across every single review, whether they liked the show or not: Karisma Kapoor is extraordinary in it. Midgard Times, which gave the show a brutal 4 out of 10, conceded that "she alone is almost worth the whole ordeal."

That kind of critical consensus — where the lead actor is the one thing everyone agrees on — doesn't happen often. It happened with Irrfan in The Lunchbox. It happened with Tabu in Andhadhun. Karisma just put herself in that conversation.

Kolkata as Co-Star

Abhinay Deo made a choice that changes everything about how the show feels: Kolkata's heat is not a production problem to be solved. It is encoded into Rita Brown's body. She sweats. She tugs at her hair. She reaches for the glass. The camera doesn't flinch, and neither does Karisma.

The original novel's detective was Bengali. Deo's adaptation reimagined her as Anglo-Indian — a community with deep roots in Kolkata that is almost never centred in Indian storytelling. This gives Rita a specific kind of cultural loneliness, an accent that is entirely her own, and a reason for the particular way she moves through the city's corridors of power without ever fully belonging to them.

The supporting cast — Jisshu Sengupta as a psychiatrist, Surya Sharma as her fellow investigator, Soni Razdan, and the legendary Helen in a comeback role — orbits around Karisma without ever trying to compete. They know whose show this is.

The Diaspora Watch

Brown is streaming on ZEE5, which is available internationally — US, UK, Canada, and 190+ countries. For diaspora audiences, this is exactly the kind of show worth a weekend binge. Seven episodes, no filler runtime inflation, a Kolkata you can practically smell through the screen.

Is it a perfect show? No. The mystery sags in the middle episodes, and the resolution won't shock anyone who has seen enough Scandi-noir. But it's a show where one of Bollywood's biggest stars of the '90s walks into a room looking nothing like herself and makes you forget every dance number she ever did. That's worth your time.

Karisma Kapoor is 51. She has nothing left to prove. She proved it anyway.
